Article Title: American billionaire Mark Cuban to CEOs: Stop getting ‘shocked’ by healthcare costs, turn to your HR Head as HR is …
Article Text:
Hidden costs in healthcare contracts



AI as a solution



Read Mark Cuban’s complete post here



CEOs turn to their Head of HR. HR is understaffed. They are being asked to take care of all their employees and families and all the issues associated with keeping them as healthy and sane and productive give as possible.

It’s an impossible job.

When I talk to that Head of HR, they say they have to trust the big insurance carriers who are their ASO and PBM. They have no choice but to

On one hand their members are terrified to change their insurance carriers for fear of losing their doctor, or other continuity issues

The vertically integrated conglomerates that own the ASO, PBM, ClearingHouse and so many more companies that have contracts with the employer , know they are afraid to change , so they take advantage

Even when that employer uses a consultant or broker , there is probably a 50pct or greater chance the broker/consultant doesn’t want to go through the work of changing, they would rather collect their fees and not change.

There are even reporting requirements (Form 5500) to disclose these costs, but the ceo has no clue about them.

All this leads to lack of change. Even when every penny they save goes right to the bottom line and increases their stock price

What I told a ceo today ? Take a off of all of your healthcare contracts and put it in your Claude , ChatGPT, grok, Gemini, whatever and use this prompt

“Where are they ripping me off “

They are always shocked.

American billionaire and entrepreneur Mark Cuban has urged the US CEOs to rethink how they manage employee healthcare, warning that executives are overspending because they lack visibility into complex insurance contracts. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Cuban said leaders often turn to their HR leads, who are “understaffed” and overwhelmed. “They are being asked to take care of all their employees and families and all the issues associated with keeping them as healthy and sane and productive as possible,” he wrote.Cuban also argued that vertically integrated conglomerates which own administrative service organisations (ASOs), pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and clearinghouses — exploit employers’ reluctance to switch providers. Brokers and consultants, he added, often discourage changes because of the extra work involved. “The vertically integrated conglomerates… know they are afraid to change, so they take advantage,” Cuban said.Cuban recommended CEOs use AI tools to review healthcare contracts and uncover hidden costs. “What I told a CEO today? Take all of your healthcare contracts and put it in your Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, whatever and use this prompt: ‘Where are they ripping me off?’ They are always shocked,” he wrote.
Article Summary: CEOs are overspending because they lack visibility into complex insurance contracts, says Mark Cuban. Cuban said leaders often turn to their HR leads, who are ‘understaffed’ and overwhelmed. “The vertically integrated conglomerates… know they are afraid to change, so they take advantage,” Cuban said.

Article Title: This $500-million superyacht’s radar shields are so huge, its crew looks like insects cleaning them; Marc Newson, famous for his work on Apple Watch, designed it for Japanese billionaire
Article Text:
$500-million Nausicaa superyacht's radar shields are huge that its crew looks like insects cleaning them

Superyacht designed by former Apple Watch designer

What are the massive domes on Nausicaä superyacht

Nausicaä superyacht is a high-tech floating resort

A viral video of Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa ’s $500 million sailing superyacht, Nausicaä, is sweeping the internet. While mega-yachts are no rarity among the elite and tech founders, this 374-foot vessel is turning heads for an unusual reason: the staggering scale of its onboard satellite equipment. Several photos and videos across Instagram and X (previously Twitter) show crew members using long-handled brushes and hoses appear almost insect-sized as they scrub the bases of four massive gray radar domes mounted near the mast.Delivered by German shipbuilder Lürssen after nearly six years of construction, the 374-foot-8-inch (114.2-meter) vessel was designed by renowned industrial designer Marc Newson, famous for his work on the Apple Watch. Instead of concealing the oversized communications equipment, Newson incorporated the four giant spheres directly into the yacht's aesthetic, creating a futuristic silhouette. Positioned directly behind the satellite array is the yacht’s black "Skydome," which houses Maezawa’s private office.The large structures are radomes (radar/antenna domes), radio-transparent, protective shells that shield delicate satellite receivers from harsh marine environments like salt water, heavy winds and rain.Inside each dome sits a satellite dish mounted on a gyro-stabilized platform that constantly shifts with the yacht's movement to maintain uninterrupted connections with orbital satellites thousands of miles away.The immense size of the radomes is due to the engineering requirements. In remote marine areas , the signal is weaker so larger dishes are required . The enclosures must be large enough for the motors and wiring inside to rotate without interference.Supporting 18 guests and up to 36 crew across 6,593 gross tons, Nausicaä operates like a floating luxury resort requiring immense digital bandwidth. In addition to guest 4K streaming and business video calls, the yacht relies on high-speed satellite links to transmit operational data.The vessel is equipped with state-of-the-art propulsion technologies, including a diesel-electric system, a 2 megawatt battery bank and a 1 megawatt methanol fuel-cell system that streams telemetry data continuously to shoreside engineers who remotely monitor vessel performance.
Article Summary: Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa’s $500 million sailing superyacht, Nausicaä, is sweeping the internet. The 374-foot-8-inch (114.2-meter) vessel was designed by renowned industrial designer Marc Newson. The large structures are radomes (radar/antenna domes), radio-transparent, protective shells.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: #TheatreReview: A story about a never-ending performance, on & off camera
Article Text:
A still from If Only

If Only

If Only

Should you watch it?





The dramaturgical perspective of society suggests that everyone is performing, constantly managing impressions depending on who is watching., written, directed and produced by Vidushi Mehra , explores this school of thought.Set in Mumbai’s Hindi film industry, it suggests that for those chasing success in showbiz, the performance never really ends. There is no backstage. The play follows four young aspirants – Aaliya, an actor grappling with insecurities beneath her success; Karam, who dreams of becoming the quintessential Bollywood hero; Anika, a photographer yearning to be seen for who she truly is; and Vedang, a writer trying to hold on to authenticity in a commercial industry.As their lives become increasingly intertwined, ambition, desire and ego blur the line between who they are and who they are expected to be, forcing each to confront secrets and choices that threaten not only their own futures but also those of the people around them. The play, staged at KNMA, Saket, examines the complexities of aspiration, identity and the pursuit of recognition. The strongest aspect of the production is its ensemble.Taarini Puri, Vivhan Mehra, Shivam Sahni and Lavanya Rathore are completely invested in their characters.The chemistry between the four actors reflects the rigour of their rehearsal process, evident in their timing, dialogue delivery, ease with one another, and nuanced emotional transitions throughout. The use of the stage space is particularly interesting. There are several moments when all four actors occupy the stage, yet the audience understands they are in entirely different locations. Without relying on elaborate sets, the actors, through precise blocking and expression, make those transitions believable.Another effective element is the live tabla by Bivas Sharma. Rather than merely accompanying the action, it punctuates emotional beats, amplifying moments of tension, introspection and drama. The music becomes an extension of the actors’ expressions. More than a story about Bollywood,is about performativity. It makes me think of Sociologist Erving Goffman’s idea in The Presentation of the Self in Everyday Life (1956) that we are all constantly performing versions of ourselves.In the entertainment industry, however, that performance seems inescapable. The characters continue to perform even when the cameras are absent, and the play captures the emotional burden of living in that perpetual state of presentation. In doing so, it encourages the audience to empathise with people in an industry that often appears glamorous on the outside but is deeply vulnerable beneath the surface. While the ending could be sharper, the play succeeds in telling an engaging, thoughtfully staged story, carried by committed performances and strong writing.Want us to review your play?Mail us at tims.delhitimes @timesofindia.com
Article Summary: If Only is written, directed and produced by Vidushi Mehra. Set in Mumbai’s Hindi film industry, it suggests that for those chasing success in showbiz, the performance never really ends. The play examines the complexities of aspiration, identity and the pursuit of recognition.

Article Title: NDMC opens first AI lab at Navyug School
Article Text: New Delhi: In a first for any govt school in Delhi, New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) opened an AR & VR Lab at Navyug School in Sarojini Nagar Friday.The place can be accessed by students of classes VI to X and used as a learning centre to connect with emerging technologies and make subjects more engaging, practical and effective.An AR & VR lab is a dedicated space featuring augmented and virtual reality hardware, software, and tools used to create immersive educational, research, and industrial experiences.NDMC vice chairperson Kuljeet Chahal said that the lab, to be known as ‘Viksit Bharat Anubhavshala’, is equipped with specially curated digital content covering more than 70 CBSE curricular and co-curricular topics.“Here, students will be able to understand technologies such as AI, Quantum Computing, Robotics, Space Science and Nanotechnology. Based on response, we will work to establish facility in other schools also. While students will understand how AI models are developed and how they function, AI-enabled learning systems will make the learning experience more engaging, interactive, personalised and effective,” he said.NDMC also plans to establish similar labs where students or children not studying in their schools can also come and access modern equipment.
Article Summary: New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) opened an AR & VR Lab at Navyug School in Sarojini Nagar. The place can be accessed by students of classes VI to X and used as a learning centre. The lab is equipped with specially curated digital content covering more than 70 CBSE curricular and co-curricular topics.

Article Title: Maths of a face: Chennai cops get new app to unmask suspects:
Article Text:
arrest





Sub-inspector Prakash walked through a maze of lanes and bylanes in Otteri last week searching for Munniyan, a ganja peddler. He had passed the suspect, but returned empty-handed. Reason: Munniyan tonsured his head and changed his appearance to escape the officer’s eye.A week later, police returned to the locality carrying a smartphone with IDENTIX app. Prakash opened the app and scanned the lanes for Munniyan’s face. Before long, the peddler was identified despite the shaved head, leading to his arrest. This new tech has the potential to substantially improve criminal investigation.Police have uploaded about 5,300 criminal profiles to the Amazon cloud database. Each person’s profile stores up to five photographs covering frontal, left, right and other views.A street search now reaches the cloud database within seconds, and IDENTIX (Identity and Intelligence) connects field policing with Amazon Rekognition’s facial-search service. Those angles matter when a face is captured from the side or another difficult position. Investigators can upload a CCTV frame, use a phone camera or submit photographs through IDENTIX on authenticated Android or iOS devices.Amazon Rekognition first locates the face in the uploaded image. It then converts the face into a numerical pattern that computers can compare. “The original photographs remain attached to each criminal profile. Amazon stores their numerical patterns in a searchable database and checks the new face against existing records,” said P Vasudevan, a facial recognition expert.“The system ranks the nearest profiles and applies an 85% similarity threshold. A record appears as a possible match only when its score crosses that level,” he said.Police said the existing face recognition system was time-consuming and returned about 20 similar records. That system ran on police servers and depended mainly on clear frontal photographs. IDENTIX uses cloud processing and can work with several reference angles.A senior police officer from Greater Chennai Police (GCP) said, “When we get a crime video footage, we can now upload it and promptly check whether the suspect involved matches anyone in our records,” he said. The platform connects 9,751 active cases and records of 562 narcotics offenders. Police said it also carries profiles of history-sheeters placed under watch across the city.The app, developed on the orders of Chennai city commissioner of police A Amalraj, will be used by special wings, beat patrol teams and officers across crime hotspots.IDENTIX can alert field teams when a possible match involves someone on a priority watchlist. This could help trace offenders outside areas where local officers know them. “The technology does not establish guilt. An app-generated match remains a lead, which investigators and senior officers must verify through case records and other evidence,” said Amarnath, a technology expert.Police plan to expand IDENTIX in phases. Future versions may connect directly with CCTV cameras and video feeds, reducing the need to extract and upload frames manually.
Article Summary: Police have uploaded about 5,300 criminal profiles to the Amazon cloud database. Each person’s profile stores up to five photographs covering frontal, left, right and other views. A street search now reaches the cloud database within seconds. The platform connects 9,751 active cases and records of 562 narcotics offenders.

Article Title: Loud mobile audio on govt buses banned in Coimbatore; earphones mandated
Article Text:
Representative image





COIMBATORE: Passengers travelling on Tamil Nadu government buses in Coimbatore have been barred from playing music or watching videos at a high volume on mobile phones, with the transport department directing commuters to use Bluetooth devices, earphones or headphones to avoid disturbing co-passengers.The department has issued fresh travel norms to ensure a quiet and safe commute, citing Rule 5(10) of the Motor Vehicle (Driving) Regulation Rules, 2017, which requires drivers to ensure that loud music is not played inside buses. It also cited Rule 228 of the Tamil Nadu Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, under which acts causing inconvenience or hardship to other passengers are treated as misconduct.As per the instructions, passengers are advised to avoid speaking continuously in a loud voice during the journey and to refrain from playing songs or watching videos on phone speakers without earphones or headphones. Mobile phone use is to be done only through Bluetooth, earphones or headphones, without affecting other passengers’ peace.The department has ordered that awareness stickers reading “No ‘speaker sound’ on mobile phones!” be pasted prominently inside all buses — at the front, middle and rear — for clear visibility. Drivers, conductors and supervisors are to be briefed on the directions at the start of duty.The curbs have come into effect immediately, and transport units have been told to send reports with photographic proof of sticker installation to the govt and the head office.TNSTC Coimbatore division has begun to past stickers on buses. The exercise will cover on 2,510 buses in Coimbatore, Tirupur, Nilgiris and Erode districts. This includes 1,100 buses in Coimbatore district.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu government buses in Coimbatore barred from playing music or watching videos at a high volume on mobile phones. Transport department has issued fresh travel norms to ensure a quiet and safe commute. Mobile phone use is to be done only through Bluetooth, earphones or headphones, without affecting other passengers’ peace.

Article Title: Madurai hospital introduces new robotic surgical system

Article Title: Japanese proverb of the day: Why "If in a hurry, take the roundabout path" teaches that slowing down is often the fastest way forward
Article Text:
Image: AI Generated

Japanese proverb of the day

"If in a hurry, take the roundabout path."

What does this proverb mean

Haste often creates the very delays we hope to avoid

Careful preparation is rarely wasted

Patience is a form of wisdom

Why this proverb still matters today

When time is running short, our first instinct is usually to rush. We cut corners, skip important steps and look for the quickest route to our destination. Yet haste often leads to mistakes that take far longer to fix than the time we thought we were saving. The Japanese proverb, "If in a hurry, take the roundabout path," offers a surprising but timeless piece of wisdom. It suggests that patience and careful planning often produce better results than speed alone. By taking the safer, steadier route, we are more likely to reach our destination without unnecessary setbacks.Rooted in Japan's tradition of valuing discipline, mindfulness and thoughtful action, the proverb reminds us that true efficiency is not about moving as fast as possible; it is about making progress without creating avoidable problems along the way. Its enduring lesson is that slowing down at the right moment can ultimately save time, reduce mistakes and lead to more reliable success in both everyday life and long-term pursuits.The proverb teaches that rushing through important tasks often increases the risk of mistakes, delays and poor decisions. Taking a little extra time to plan carefully, prepare properly and work methodically may seem slower at first, but it usually saves time in the long run.The saying encourages patience, attention to detail and the understanding that lasting success is built on careful action rather than reckless speed.When people feel pressured by time, they are more likely to overlook details, make careless errors or choose shortcuts that backfire. A rushed email may contain costly mistakes, hurried construction can compromise safety and impulsive decisions often require even more effort to correct later. The proverb reminds us that many delays are not caused by moving too slowly but by moving too quickly without thinking.Athletes train for months before competitions, pilots complete detailed safety checks before every flight and surgeons follow strict procedures before an operation begins. These moments of preparation may appear time-consuming, but they reduce the likelihood of serious problems later. Taking the "roundabout path" does not mean avoiding action, it means laying a strong foundation before moving forward.Choosing the longer route is not always a sign of hesitation. Sometimes it reflects experience. People who have faced setbacks understand that steady progress often outlasts rushed success. Whether building a career, learning a new skill or making an important life decision, patience allows us to think clearly, adapt when necessary and avoid unnecessary risks. In many cases, what seems like the slower choice turns out to be the most efficient one.Modern life often rewards speed. We expect instant replies, same-day deliveries and quick results in almost every aspect of life. Yet many of the things that matter most, earning trust, mastering a profession, building meaningful relationships or creating something of lasting value, cannot be rushed. This Japanese proverb reminds us that slowing down is not the opposite of progress. The enduring lesson behind the saying is that when the stakes are high, taking the thoughtful path is often the quickest way to reach the destination without losing your way.
Article Summary: The Japanese proverb, "If in a hurry, take the roundabout path," offers a surprising but timeless piece of wisdom. Rooted in Japan's tradition of valuing discipline, mindfulness and thoughtful action, the proverb reminds us that true efficiency is not about moving as fast as possible.

Article Title: In 1952, Canada began spraying forests from aeroplanes to control budworms; decades later, pesticide research changed how forests were managed
Article Text:
New Brunswick extensively used aerial pesticide spraying for spruce budworm outbreaks. Aircraft applied chemicals over vast forest areas between 1952 and 1993. Growing scientific understanding of pesticide impacts altered forest management regulations. Image Credits: Natural Resources Canada

Why Canada resorted to aerial spraying for the spruce budworm

Impact of evolving knowledge on forest management

This evolving knowledge led to more careful and alternative pest control approaches. Canada's experience highlights the connection between forest health and human needs. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Lessons learned in Canada’s forests

Forests are often seen as untouched by human decision-making. According to The Natural Resources Canada article , spruce budworm outbreaks have been one of the most significant challenges for forest managers in Canada because the insects feed on fir and spruce trees, causing widespread damage during outbreaks.The Natural Resources Canada article explains how pesticide use developed in New Brunswick, why it was used and how changing scientific knowledge altered forest management. According to the Natural Resources Canada article, aerial spraying was used extensively in New Brunswick to manage spruce budworm outbreaks, with pesticide applications carried out over large forest areas between 1952 and 1993. The article notes that growing scientific understanding of pesticide impacts led to changes in regulations and influenced how forest management practices evolved.New Brunswick’s forests were central to the spruce budworm management efforts described in the Natural Resources Canada article on historical pesticide use. The province used aerial pesticide spraying to respond to insect outbreaks that threatened its forests. Natural Resources Canada notes that spruce budworm outbreaks affected extensive areas of spruce and fir forests in New Brunswick, prompting aerial pesticide spraying programmes as a management response.The outbreaks were a problem because damaged trees could reduce productivity.To respond to these outbreaks, forest managers used pesticides to reduce spruce budworm populations. Beginning in the 1950s, aircraft were used to spray large forest areas because they could cover wide regions quickly.According to Natural Resources Canada, aerial pesticide spraying was used as a management tool during spruce budworm outbreaks in New Brunswick, as authorities sought to reduce insect populations and protect affected forests. Pesticides became a major part of forest management programmes because they offered a fast response when insect populations increased.According to Natural Resources Canada, pesticides were used in Canadian forests to control insect pests from 1945 onwards, and DDT was among the insecticides applied during large-scale forest management programmes to control eastern spruce budworm outbreaks in New Brunswick. It was widely used in pest control programmes because it was effective against insects and remained active for long periods. However, as more research became available, scientists and environmental authorities better understood the wider effects of persistent chemicals in the environment. New Brunswick’s pesticide history shows how forest management strategies changed as new information emerged.The Natural Resources Canada article says forest pesticide use depended heavily on the science available at the time. As concerns about some chemicals grew, forest managers began exploring alternative strategies.According to Natural Resources Canada, evolving scientific knowledge about pesticide impacts changed how forest pest management was approached. Managing one species can have wider effects that are not immediately obvious.Natural Resources Canada says changing scientific knowledge about pesticide use influenced forest management practices. Instead of relying only on broad pesticide applications, forest managers increasingly considered other methods and used scientific evidence to guide decisions.The article says pesticide regulations and management practices changed as researchers learned more about environmental impacts. These changes show that conservation and forestry practices continue to evolve.Spruce budworm infestations occur naturally in forests, but when populations grow, they can become a problem for people who depend on the forest for their livelihoods.New Brunswick’s spruce budworm history highlights the challenge of balancing environmental protection with human needs. Protecting forests also means considering the wider environment.Natural Resources Canada explains that aerial pesticide spraying was used in New Brunswick to manage spruce budworm outbreaks during a period when chemical treatments were widely used in forest protection programmes. Over time, improved scientific understanding changed how those decisions were made and led to more careful approaches.Canada’s experience with historical pesticide use suggests that protecting forests involves more than controlling one threat. It requires understanding how trees, insects, wildlife and human activity are connected.New Brunswick’s forests still show the tension between protection and caution. Natural Resources Canada notes that increased scientific understanding of pesticide impacts has changed forest pest management practices.
Article Summary: New Brunswick extensively used aerial pesticide spraying for spruce budworm outbreaks. Aircraft applied chemicals over vast forest areas between 1952 and 1993. Growing scientific understanding of pesticide impacts altered forest management regulations. Canada’s experience with historical pesticide use suggests that protecting forests involves more than controlling one threat.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bertrand Russell: 'There are two motives for reading a book; one, that you enjoy it; the other...' and how most of us are guilty of the second
Article Text:
Bertrand Russell was a British philosopher, logician, mathematician, and one of the most influential thinkers of the 20th century.

"There are two motives for reading a book; one, that you enjoy it; the other, that you can boast about it,"

A philosopher’s critique of modern anxiety

The psychology of social performance

Performative reading in the digital age

Finding the private joy in pages

Walk into a crowded coffee shop or scroll through social media, and you will quickly spot a familiar ritual. A heavy paperbound volume of James Joyce’s Ulysses or David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest lies open on a small wooden table. Its owner glances around, sips an espresso, and leaves the spine clearly visible to passersby.wrote British philosopher Bertrand Russell in his 1930 book The Conquest of Happiness.Russell captured a quiet truth about human behaviour. Reading serves two completely different masters: private satisfaction and public status. While we like to imagine that every turned page stems from pure curiosity, our desire for intellectual prestige often drives us to pick up books we have no real intention of finishing.Russell wrote The Conquest of Happiness during a period of massive social change in post-World War I Britain. As literacy rates climbed and mass-market publishing expanded across Europe, books became accessible consumer goods rather than rare luxuries.In a chapter titled Byronic Unhappiness, Russell analyzed how modern urban life encouraged superficial intellectualism. People bought dense philosophical treatises and classic literature not to absorb their ideas, but to signal membership in an educated upper class.Russell’s target was not reading itself. As a logician who co-wrote the three-volume mathematical landmark Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead, he valued rigorous study. Instead, he targeted the widespread anxiety caused by doing things purely for social approval. He argued that reading out of obligation or vanity turned a potentially joyful habit into exhausting performance art.Russell’s distinction connects directly to simple psychological ideas about human motivation.In the 1970s, psychologists Edward L. Deci and Richard M. Ryan developed Self-Determination Theory. This idea separates two types of motivation: intrinsic motivation (doing an activity simply because you enjoy it) and extrinsic motivation (doing something to gain outside rewards, attention, or status). Reading for personal fun is a classic intrinsic activity. Reading to build an impressive public reputation relies entirely on extrinsic social approval.Sociologist Pierre Bourdieu explored this same tension in his 1979 book Distinction: A Social Critique of the Judgement of Taste. Bourdieu showed how educated groups use cultural knowledge, including familiar books, classical music, and fine art, to mark subtle boundaries between social classes. Displaying a thick, challenging book serves as a silent signal of leisure time, education, and high standing.When people buy books primarily to brag about them, they fall into what social psychologist Erich Fromm called the "having mode" of existence. Instead of entering the "being mode," which means engaging deeply with an author's ideas and allowing those ideas to shape their worldview, they treat books as physical trophies to collect and show off.Russell's observation hits harder today than when he published it nearly a century ago. Digital platforms have turned reading into a tracked, public performance sport.On social media platforms like Goodreads, users publicly display annual reading goals, logging 50 or 100 books a year in a race against arbitrary numbers. On Instagram and TikTok, short video creators build personal channels around carefully arranged bookshelf tours, color-coordinated book displays, and monthly reading wrap-up videos. The term "tsundoku," which is a Japanese word for buying books and letting them pile up unread, has become a popular badge of honor online.This performative culture creates measurable changes in reading habits. Pierre Bayard, a literature professor at the University of Paris VIII, published an honest study in 2007 titled How to Talk About Books You Haven't Read. Bayard noted that in academic and social circles, people routinely pretend to have read major classics to protect their social standing and avoid looking uneducated.When readers choose books based on what looks impressive on a digital profile, they often abandon books that offer genuine personal delight. Easy fiction, light mysteries, and graphic novels get pushed aside in favor of lengthy biographies or dense histories that sit half-read on bedside tables.When reading becomes a public performance, it loses its power to rest the mind. Trying to read books you dislike just to impress strangers turns a peaceful hobby into another source of daily stress.Russell believed that true happiness requires direct, unforced engagement with the world. Reading for genuine pleasure allows a person to lose track of time, enter new ideas, and learn without keeping score. It provides a rare quiet space where you do not need to prove anything to anyone.A room full of unread books is not a personal failure, provided those books were chosen with real curiosity rather than vanity. The true value of a personal library lies not in how impressive it looks to visitors, but in how deeply its contents belong to the reader sitting quietly in the chair.
Article Summary: Bertrand Russell wrote The Conquest of Happiness during a period of massive social change in post-World War I Britain. He argued that reading out of obligation or vanity turned a potentially joyful habit into exhausting performance art. Digital platforms have turned reading into a tracked, public performance sport. Reading for genuine pleasure allows a person to lose track of time and learn new ideas.

Article Title: A switchable window coating can heat buildings by 33°C or cool them below ambient, and lab tests suggest it could cut HVAC energy use in some U.S. climates
Article Text:
Researchers developed an innovative electrochromic material for buildings. This material switches between absorbing solar energy and emitting heat to space. Lab tests showed significant temperature differences during heating and cooling modes. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

One coating to fit all seasons

The way the coating manages to produce heating and cooling effects

Simulations suggest substantial HVAC energy savings in various US climates. Further research aims to improve durability and scalability for widespread adoption. Image Credits: Electrochromic Adaptive Solar Heater and Sub-AmbientPassive Daytime Radiative Cooler study

Simulations reveal energy savings potential

Keeping homes and offices comfortable all year round is not without the use of significant amounts of energy. Buildings consume about 30% of the total energy consumed worldwide, while HVAC (Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning) consume almost 17% of the energy consumption in buildings, according to an investigation by the journal Advanced Materials . In trying to find ways for countries to cut emissions without compromising indoor comfort, there have been efforts from researchers to come up with materials for buildings that could adapt to weather changes.According to research, an innovative switchable electrochromic material has been developed that is capable of switching between absorbing energy from the sun in cold months and emitting energy to space in warm months. During lab tests and outdoor demonstration tests, the material was able to achieve temperatures that were about 33°C above ambient during heating mode and 1°C below ambient temperature during cooling mode during daytime. Simulations performed by the scientists show that the new material can help save HVAC energy consumption in some parts of the US.Many coatings are already available in the market, but each of these coatings serves only one purpose. Some coatings are reflective in nature, which helps to keep buildings cool, whereas other coatings can absorb solar radiation and help to add some extra heat.The problem is that climate varies with changing seasons.The researchers behind the Advanced Materials study aimed to solve this problem by creating a coating that can switch between heating and cooling modes whenever needed. Instead of using moving parts, the material changes its behaviour when a small electrical voltage is applied.In cooling mode, the coating reflects most incoming sunlight while efficiently releasing heat through passive daytime radiative cooling. In heating mode, it absorbs much more solar energy while reducing heat loss, allowing the surface to warm considerably under sunlight.One feature highlighted in the study is that the coating is non-volatile. After switching into either heating or cooling mode, it remains in that state even when the electrical power is turned off. Electricity is required only to change between the two modes rather than to maintain them continuously.As mentioned by the scientists, this feature can make the technology appealing to buildings, as it will allow making adjustments in seasons using electricity for just a few moments rather than constantly.This coating consists of ultrathin graphene with engineered copper-bismuth nanoclusters, which gives it two distinct thermal properties. As claimed by the scientists, traditional electrochromics find it hard to control the radiation from the sunlight and mid-infrared heat radiation simultaneously.To overcome this challenge, the team developed a manufacturing process that deposits amorphous copper-bismuth nanoclusters onto defect-activated monolayer graphene. According to the study, this structure enables a strong contrast between the heating and cooling states.When operating in cooling mode, the material absorbed only about 8% of incoming solar energy while maintaining very high thermal emissivity, allowing it to release heat efficiently. In heating mode, solar absorption increased to nearly 48%, while thermal emissivity dropped substantially, helping retain warmth.The researchers also modified the graphene surface to improve the uniformity of the deposited metal layer. They combined this with a pulse electrodeposition technique that helped produce a more even coating without introducing additional materials that could reduce cooling performance by absorbing unwanted sunlight.Laboratory durability tests showed that the device continued to switch reversibly for more than 1,000 cycles. The authors observed some gradual performance degradation over repeated cycling and suggest that future electrolyte designs could improve long-term durability.To evaluate the technology outside the laboratory, the team carried out an outdoor proof-of-concept test on the rooftop of Stanford University's Electrical Engineering Building. During the daytime experiment, the cooling mode lowered the device temperature to approximately 1°C below the surrounding air, while the heating mode raised it by an average of about 33°C above ambient temperature.The authors observe that such outdoor tests should be regarded as proof of concept of the technology, but not as an indication of its readiness for mass commercialisation.In order to assess the performance of the technology on buildings, the authors applied EnergyPlus software – a whole-building energy simulation tool – to simulate a mid-rise apartment with the adaptive coating in different U.S. climates.The simulations suggest that switching between heating and cooling modes according to weather conditions could reduce annual HVAC energy consumption by an average of 73.69 MBtu in the simulated scenarios. The projected savings were greater in warmer climates, where passive radiative cooling has a larger impact on reducing cooling demand.The researchers also estimated that the adaptive coating could reduce annual carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 4,063 kilograms per building in the simulated U.S. scenarios. They attribute this mainly to lower electricity demand for cooling, while noting that the estimates are based on building simulations rather than real-world deployment.Although the results are encouraging, the authors emphasise that further work is needed before the technology can be used widely. They identify improving durability, increasing manufacturing scalability and enhancing heating performance in colder climates as important next steps.The study also notes that scaling the graphene electrode to larger areas presents engineering challenges because electrical resistance increases across bigger surfaces. Future research will focus on refining the materials, improving long-term reliability and making the technology more practical for large-scale applications.Building coatings that switch between heat absorption and reflection could improve energy efficiency if further research confirms their performance. The technology should not be considered as an alternative to existing HVAC systems; instead, it may assist buildings in adjusting better to weather conditions.
Article Summary: Researchers developed an innovative electrochromic material for buildings. This material switches between absorbing solar energy and emitting heat to space. Lab tests showed significant temperature differences during heating and cooling modes. Simulations suggest substantial HVAC energy savings in various US climates. Further research aims to improve durability and scalability for widespread adoption.

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: Before the knowledge walks out the door
Article Text:
Everyone in Silicon Valley is racing to build machines that replace human expertise.

Ahmer Inam

, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it.

When Ahmer Inam appeared on Fox & Friends in June, his mother watched the segment without following much of it. Her English is limited. There was her son on the famous curved couch of American morning television, fielding questions about artificial intelligence, and she understood almost none of the words. She wept anyway. Some distances need no translation, and the one between a schoolteacher's household in Delhi and a Manhattan television studio is legible in any language.Had she followed the argument, it might have surprised her less than it surprised the audience. Because what Inam was defending, underneath the vocabulary of frontier AI, is approximately the oldest idea in civilisation — the one his father practised for a living: that knowledge survives only when one generation troubles to hand it to the next.Inam has spent twenty-five years building artificial intelligence — long enough to remember when it meant symbolic logic in the late nineties, and senior enough to have run AI and data for Fortune 500 companies, Nike and Wells Fargo among them, back when "chief AI officer" was still an exotic title. He is not, in other words, a critic sniping from the cheap seats. Which makes the thesis of Cognisee, the research lab he founded and leads, sound almost seditious in today's Silicon Valley: "We're not trying to replace the worker," he says."We're trying to make the worker irreplaceable."The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage." By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030 — electricians, welders, machinists, the hands America needs if it is serious about building factories, chip plants and grid capacity again. But Inam's diagnosis is sharper than a headcount. "America does not have a work shortage," he likes to say. "It has an expertise shortage."Consider what actually leaves the building when a master electrician retires at sixty-eight. Not the manual — the manual stays. What leaves is the ear that catches a motor running slightly wrong two weeks before it fails; the instinct that connects a faint vibration to a pattern in old maintenance logs; forty years of judgment that was never written down because it could not be. The philosopher Michael Polanyi had a name for this — tacit knowledge, the things we know but cannot tell — and Cognisee is, at bottom, a bet that the most valuable training data on earth is tacit.The company's method has a fable-like symmetry. Its AI begins as an apprentice: it works alongside experienced people and learns what they notice, what they ask, how they make judgment calls. Then it turns around and becomes a coach, carrying that accumulated judgment to the newcomer. "First it's an apprentice," Inam says. "Then it becomes a coach." Picture a 22-year-old on his first aircraft-maintenance job, hearing a sound he has never heard before, with the distilled instincts of the country's best technicians beside him in real time. "He's not being replaced by a machine," Inam says. "He's being mentored by one."The repository where all this lives is called, a little grandly, a Wisdom Vault — a secure library of hard-won know-how from doctors, nurses, electricians, factory workers, farmers, small-business owners. Grand or not, the name gives away the emotional register Inam is working in. This is not pitched as workforce optimisation. It is pitched as inheritance.He is careful — insistent, actually — about the question that framing invites: who owns it? In Cognisee's design, the expert decides what to preserve, what to share, and with whom; the contributor is recognised and rewarded; the knowledge belongs to the person who earned it, not to the machine that absorbed it. "There is a big difference," Inam says, "between being monitored and being mentored." The company is incorporated as a public benefit corporation, which he describes as a legal commitment to the worker rather than a marketing pledge.That ownership principle is also where his quarrel with the reigning AI paradigm becomes explicit. The frontier labs, Inam argues, got intelligent by swallowing the written internet — and the written internet is now substantially swallowed, which is why the industry's plan increasingly amounts to bigger data centres and more electricity, even as some of the field's own pioneers warn of a wall ahead. His contrarian wager is that the next leap will come not from more compute but from the knowledge that never made it onto the internet in the first place — and that it can be gathered by consent rather than by crawler.For an Indian reader, the resonance is hard to miss. This is a country that has watched its weaves, its remedies and its craft knowledge catalogued, carried off and sold back to it before. It is also a country whose deepest teaching traditions were never textual at all, but moved from person to person — the guru-shishya parampara, the ustad and the shagird. Inam has spoken about Wisdom Vaults for indigenous and medicinal knowledge, with communities retaining ownership of what they contribute. One way to describe Cognisee is as an attempt to give the world's oral inheritances an infrastructure layer — sovereignty included.The idea is attracting converts from unexpected quarters. Cognisee's co-founder, Alex Giannou, spent nearly two decades on Wall Street financing precisely the data centres and power deals behind the AI boom; he crossed over, in Inam's telling, because the right bet and the smart bet turned out to be the same one. Among the company's early backers is a senior Google executive who helped invent federated learning, one of the foundational privacy-preserving techniques of modern machine learning. And last year the XPRIZE Foundation, where Inam serves as a Visionary, recognised his work with its Global Visioneering Award.None of which quite explains the conviction. For that you have to go back to Delhi. Inam grew up in a low-income household, the son of a teacher — a man who spent his working life on the least scalable expertise-transfer technology ever devised: one adult, one room, one generation at a time. The son's journey to America was not gilded; there were stretches, early on, when he could not always afford to eat. It takes a particular kind of person to emerge from that and conclude that a nation's most undervalued asset sits not in its server farms but in the heads of its retiring machinists and nurses."Every generation should start where the last one left off," Inam says. It sounds like a product principle. It is closer to a family creed — the thing his father practised without ever calling it a thesis, the thing his mother recognised on a television screen in a language she does not speak. Some knowledge, it turns out, transfers just fine.
Article Summary: Ahmer Inam, a schoolteacher's son from Delhi, is building machines that inherit it. The problem he is aiming at usually gets filed under the bland heading of "labour shortage" By one estimate, more than two million skilled-trade jobs in the United States could sit unfilled by 2030.

Article Title: Bill Gates' daughter Phoebe Gates' shopping app Phia is in damage control mode after revelations that 'shocked' many
Article Text:
Phia claimed sales it never drove. Now it is paying brands back

Phia cookie stuffing explained: how fake clicks let a shopping app claim commissions it never earned

Phia calls it a bug, investigation calls it auto_drop: the December 2025 code that ran for seven months

Impact.com suspends Phia as refunds begin, while Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni say nothing

Phia, the shopping app co-founded by Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni, is now issuing refunds and reversing transactions after admitting it collected commissions on sales it never actually drove. Business Insider reported that the startup is working with affiliate network Impact.com to correct attributions, and a Phia spokesperson confirmed the company has offered transaction reversals to brands. Impact.com said it is reprocessing every action credited to Phia between June 20 and July 29 that had not yet been paid out, reattributing them to the right publisher or refunding advertisers.The cleanup follows a Bloomberg investigation published on July 9 that found Phia's mobile browser extension quietly opening a background tab during checkout and injecting its own referral code, overwriting whoever had actually sent the shopper there. Bloomberg tested the extension across more than 50 retail sites, including Walmart, Nike and Zara. In one test, clicking a Nordstrom link from a Wirecutter article triggered a background tab that swapped Wirecutter's affiliate code for Phia's.The practice has a name in the industry: cookie stuffing, or forced clicks.Affiliate marketing runs on one rule, that a commission is owed only when a user actually clicks a link and then buys. Independent researcher Ben Edelman, who reviewed Phia's public code and ran his own tests, found a setting called enable_coupon_auto_drop that fired affiliate links without any user action, usually at the cart or checkout page. Crucially, it was switched on only for iOS users through a server-side feature flag, which is why desktop-only testers missed it for months.Capital One Shopping, which makes a rival extension, reached the same conclusion and emailed retailers with video evidence. Publishers were losing real revenue, the email said, and advertisers were paying for fake clicks.Phia has called it a bug. Its spokesperson told Bloomberg the company learned that a recent release was causing misattributions from a subset of users, and that the team worked overnight to fix it. Bloomberg retested after contacting the company on July 7 and found the automatic referral claims had stopped.Edelman disputes the framing. The feature first shipped in version 1.9.33 on December 13, 2025, which puts it in the field for roughly seven months, including the holiday shopping season. A feature named auto_drop that automatically drops affiliate cookies, he argues, is hard to describe as an accident.The stakes are high for a company that has raised $43.5 million from Kleiner Perkins, Khosla Ventures and Notable Capital, plus celebrity backers including Hailey Bieber, Khloe Kardashian, Sydney Sweeney and Sheryl Sandberg. Phia's app has been downloaded over 1.2 million times in the past year.Impact.com has temporarily suspended Phia from its marketplace, the tool brands use to find new partners, and wants a stretch of clean compliance before reinstating it. Rakuten Advertising says it is investigating. CJ Affiliate told partners it is making reconciliation payments.Gates and Kianni, who promote Phia constantly across social media and host a podcast called The Burnouts, have said nothing publicly.
Article Summary: Phia's mobile browser extension quietly opened a background tab during checkout and injected its own referral code, overwriting whoever had actually sent the shopper there. Bloomberg tested the extension across more than 50 retail sites, including Walmart, Nike and Zara. The practice has a name in the industry: cookie stuffing, or forced clicks.

Article Title: AI has drawn Google, Meta and other tech companies into construction business, making these jobs one of the highest-paid
Article Text:
Why Google and Meta are spending millions to train electricians

A training centre caught in the middle

The massive appetite for AI’s computing power is turning construction into one of the best-paying trades in the US. Google, Meta and other tech giants are now pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into training the electricians and skilled workers needed to build their data centres, a report has said.For example, one of the data centers being built in Detroit, backed by OpenAI, is being called the single biggest private investment in Michigan's history, as per a report by The New York Times, it needs hundreds of electricians working 10-hour shifts, seven days a week, and it's paying accordingly.The pull of data centre money is the main topic of conversation at the Detroit Electrical Industry Training Center, where roughly 850 apprentices are currently training, the report added. It's one of 270 such centers across the country now getting direct support from AI companies, who are pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into making sure there are enough skilled workers to build their facilities.Meanwhile, Google alone has put in $50 million through a partnership with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, aimed at nearly doubling the union's annual apprenticeship intake from 19,500 to 30,000 over the next three years, at locations Google has picked out itself.Asset management giant BlackRock has chipped in with its own grant as part of a separate $100 million push to widen training pipelines for its data centers in Texas.The report notes that the data centre growth is starting to squeeze everything around it: land and raw materials and workers. According to an analysis by the job site Indeed, hourly installation and maintenance jobs at data centers now pay 42% more than comparable roles in other industries.In hotspots like Dallas and Northern Virginia, where data centre construction is especially dense, workers can jump between projects for bigger bonuses or higher daily rates, and contractors are increasingly turning to staffing agencies like Aerotek just to keep crews fully staffed.Tech companies training their own workforce isn't newThis isn't the first time a tech company has taken on the job of training the people who keep its facilities running. Microsoft has been doing something similar since 2018, when it launched its own data center technician training programs. It now runs 39 such locations worldwide and has trained roughly 15,000 people through them.
Article Summary: Google, Meta and other tech giants are pouring millions into training electricians and skilled workers needed to build their data centres. Google alone has put in $50 million through a partnership with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. BlackRock has chipped in with its own $100 million push to widen training pipelines for its data centers in Texas.

Google has rolled back the new feature that allowed Google Earth users to generate AI visualizations on top of the service's satellite imagery. The roll back comes in lass than 24 hours after concerns from researchers and open-source intelligence experts about disinformation risks that the feature raised. The "create image" tool, rolled out Thursday (July 30), integrates Google's Nano Banana 2 image-generation technology to let users zoom into locations and build images in seconds based on Google Earth satellite, aerial and 3D-mapping data.In its initial announcement of the new feature on Thursday, the company said it was designed to work with users' imaginations: "Just zoom in to a place in Google Earth on web (sic), tap 'create image,' and type whatever you want to see," Bryan Horowitz, a product manager wrote.In a statement announcing the company's decision to pause the feature, Google said, "We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world.We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies. So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails. It's important to note that generated images didn’t appear in the main Google Earth experience for others to see and were watermarked as AI generated."Raising alarm on the feature, Henk van Ess, an open-source researcher, wrote on X, "I tried refugees at the Mexican border, a nuclear plant in Iran, a crash in Amsterdam, a hospital with a bomb crater in Gaza. Nothing was refused." Brady Africk, a research analyst at the American Enterprise Institute specializing in satellite imagery analysis, told AFP the Google Earth update "makes it easier to generate convincing fake satellite imagery that can spread quickly online and mislead the public. " "These AI-generated fakes, growing more common, may also erode public trust in satellite imagery, and make the jobs of journalists and researchers more difficult."In a response to AFP and Ess on X, Google said that the images created with the feature include SynthID digital watermarks, invisible markers embedded in media generated using the company's artificial intelligence tools. Users can ask Google's Gemini chatbot if a SynthID is present. "We take misinformation seriously – every image created with Nano Banana in Google Earth includes the SynthID digital watermark, so if someone is unsure about an image, they can ask the Gemini app or use Lens in Search to see if the image was AI-generated. In addition, we prevent image creation on harmful topics and are continually updating our protections," wrote Google.
Article Summary: Google has rolled back a new feature that allowed Google Earth users to generate AI visualizations on top of the service's satellite imagery. The roll back comes in lass than 24 hours after concerns from researchers and open-source intelligence experts about disinformation risks. Google said that the images created with the feature include SynthID digital watermarks.

Article Title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he got addicted to this ‘Larry Ellison’s app’; It got ‘too powerful’ for him
Article Text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman compared the experience to a drug

TikTok ownership change in the US

The rise and fall of OpenAI's Sora app

Even Sam Altman is not immune to the endless scrolling on TikTok. The OpenAI CEO recently revealed that he forced himself to get “addicted” to TikTok to study its mechanics only to delete the app after finding it “too powerful” to control. Speaking on a recent episode of the Relentless podcast, Altman shared how a research experiment to understand TikTok’s recommendation algorithm quickly spiraled into a personal distraction.“I made myself get addicted to TikTok, because I wanted to just learn. I really thought it was great. “And then I thought I could control it. I was like, 'Oh, it's actually kind of fun,' but I only use it for 10 minutes to wind down before bed, and I'm totally in control of it. And then it was an hour one night. And then some Saturday afternoon, I was on the couch for like three hours,” Altman said.Altman compared the experience to a drug, noting that while he was “really enjoying it in the moment,” he knew the habit was bad for him. After briefly scaling his usage down to a few minutes before bed, he decided to delete the app entirely.“I briefly got it back under control, and I was down to five, 10 minutes a night, whatever, like a little wind down before bed,” he said, adding, “Then I was just like, enough.”After years of deliberation, TikTok’s US operations are now owned by a majority-investor entity called TikTok USDS Joint Venture that includes Larry Ellison’s Oracle, Silver Lake and MGX. The global operations, however, remain tied to ByteDance, which retains a minority 19.9% share in the US venture. Meanwhile, the storage and algorithmic operations in the US are hosted securely on Oracle cloud infrastructure.Altman’s deep dive into TikTok coincided with OpenAI’s internal efforts to build its own AI-generated video social media platform, Sora. Despite generating massive hype and securing a partnership with Disney, OpenAI officially scrapped the Sora app project in March after six months of development.Company executives determined that rendering video consumed too much computing power at a time when resources were better spent competing with rivals like Anthropic in the core generative AI race.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he got addicted to TikTok to study its mechanics. Altman compared the experience to a drug, noting that while he was “really enjoying it in the moment,” he knew the habit was bad for him. After briefly scaling his usage down, he decided to delete the app entirely.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg is not convinced if OpenAI and Anthropic really want Chinese AI models in America, says: Signal is ...
Article Text:
The increasing Chinese competition



Open vs closed models



Mark Zuckerberg makes an offer to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei



Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has entered the intensifying Washington debate over whether Chinese AI models should be restricted in the US, wanting that banning them would not be ‘an effective solution’. In an interview with Financial Times, Zuckerberg said the US should compete by identifying bottlenecks and roadblocks rather than blocking rivals outright. He also cautioned against ‘regulatory capture’ by American frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which he suggested could use policy to throttle domestic competition. Zuckerberg’s remarks appeared to be a broadside against OpenAI and Anthropic, which dominate the chatbot market with proprietary closed models. He said there were “mixed signals” about whether frontier labs truly want open-source models to succeed. “Are the frontier labs going to want an open-source model to succeed? I think that there have kind of been some mixed signals on that,” he told the FT.The comments from Zuckerberg comes after Beijing-based Moonsht AI released its Kimi K3 model, whose capabilities are nearing those of OpenAI and Anthropic. US officials have also accused Moonshot of covertly training its model using distillation from American rivals, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warning that sanctions are on the table for labs that cross into intellectual property theft.Zuckerberg reiterated his support for “AI for everyone” and open models that users can customize and run on their own hardware — a popular approach among Chinese developers. He warned that AI risks becoming centralized in the hands of a few powerful groups. While Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for stronger regulation and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis has proposed a self-regulatory body, Zuckerberg said restrictions on powerful tools were not the right answer. He argued that open models could help patch cybersecurity vulnerabilities faster than closed ones.Zuckerberg’s intervention highlights a growing split among U.S. tech leaders over how to respond to Chinese competition and regulate AI. While rivals push for tighter controls, he is positioning Meta as a champion of open-source approaches — even as his company develops its own closed model, Muse Spark, citing safety concerns.In related news, recently it was reported that Meta is in early talks to lease computing power to Anthropic in a deal that could be worth as much as $10 billion over two years, according to a New York Times report. If it closes, it would hand Mark Zuckerberg a brand-new line of business and pull Dario Amodei's AI lab deeper into a scramble for compute that shows no sign of easing.The move borrows straight from Elon Musk's playbook. Musk turned SpaceX's Colossus data centers into a rental business earlier this year, and Anthropic became its anchor tenant. Now Zuckerberg wants a slice of the same action, using the very data centers his investors keep grumbling about. Anthropic pitched the idea first, in JuneThe NYT reports that Anthropic proposed the deal in June, and Meta is weighing it. Anthropic would pay in monthly instalments across two years, with either side free to opt out early. The specifics are still moving around.
Article Summary: Zuckerberg says US should compete by identifying bottlenecks and roadblocks rather than blocking rivals outright. Warns against ‘regulatory capture’ by American frontier labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, which he suggested could use policy to throttle domestic competition.
